$about: field-3 round, 2026-08-06: the third FIELD-1 repository and the first at scale - matomo-org/matomo, 13,591 tracked files, 31,287 commits since 2007-07-24, 98 plugin directories, 479 all-time authors. Run as a user would ask rather than as the author would drive: the align router's intake, then its brownfield phase's eight assessment passes, then payoff-ordered waves. Every number below was produced by running a shipped script against the adopted working copy and can be reproduced from the procedure in its case. The round's central finding is not a broken guard - every guard ran, passed, and finished in under 250 ms on 13,591 files. It is that the number the guards report stopped describing the repository.

observations.evidence: matomo's own `.gitignore:13` is `/docs/`; the file's most recent change is dated 2026-05-15, so the rule predates this run rather than being provoked by it. Sixteen of the manifest's 48 file entries live under `docs/` - including the two required ones, `docs/decision-records` and `docs/personas.md`. The adoption put 14 files there: the persona roster the R10 gate reads, five retroactive ADRs, one BDR, both stream indexes, both templates, PRODUCT.md, ARCHITECTURE.md and facts.example.json. `git check-ignore -v docs/personas.md` resolves to `.gitignore:13`; `git status --porcelain` never lists the directory; `git add -A && git commit` produced a commit of 51 files with **zero** paths under `docs/`. On that same tree `node scripts/self-verify.mjs` prints `PASS file docs/personas.md`, `PASS file docs/facts.example.json` and the verdict `self-verify: OK - drift 0 - 98% adopted (57/58), 1 excepted - compliant with the standard`. The cause is one line of self-verify's own design: `exists()` walks `readdirSync` listings, so it asks the filesystem and never the index. Its code comment explains at length why it stopped using `existsSync` (case-insensitivity made compliance depend on whose machine asked) and never asks the question one layer up - is this file in the repo at all. R3 says project knowledge must live in the repo, versioned with the code; here a third of the manifest's file entries resolve to a directory this repository will not carry, and the files sit on one laptop. The align router does name this failure mode, but only as a parenthetical about one file ('a broad settings.json .gitignore rule swallowing .claude/settings.json - add a `!` negation'), with no general rule and nothing mechanical behind it.
observations.waiver: Whether an ignored artifact is drift or a warning is a design decision with real consequences for existing adopters (it can only raise their drift), and self-verify currently uses no git at all. Options are written into the case; not guessed on the owner's behalf this round.

observations.evidence: Drift reached 0 in a single sitting on a nineteen-year, 13,591-file platform. The align router says the opposite should happen - 'wave one closes red, by design. A multi-year repo does not reach drift 0 in one pull request and must not try' - and the reason it can happen anyway is arithmetic: drift counts unmet entries of a manifest that has 48 files, 4 sections and 7 guards, none of which scales with the repository. Reaching 0 needed a personas file, a backlog, a decision-records directory, a capability map, one CI workflow, three AGENTS.md headings and one recorded exception. At `drift 0 - 98% adopted (57/58)` the same tree reports: `spec-guard --audit: 12 problem(s)` - 12 of the 14 mapped capabilities have no spec; a counted backlog of **36** items (14 specs, 9 decisions, 7 drift reconciliations, 6 guards); and the unclaimed-code check switched off, so 13,591 files were never examined. FIELD-1's small target moved 14 -> 0 with all three of its capabilities specced and `spec-guard --audit` reporting `78 files, each claimed by a capability or declared unclaimed`; here the identical 0 coexists with 36 items, twelve unwritten specs and an unclaimed check that is off. The two numbers are not comparable and nothing in the output says so. Worth stating precisely what did not fail: the drift number is *reproducible* and *honest about what it measures* - it never claimed to measure the repository. The defect is that the align router's own re-entry section names it as the progress bar ('Close each wave with self-verify; the number falling is the progress bar'), and at this size it is a progress bar that fills up in the first hour of a programme measured in months.
observations.waiver: Fixing this means either a manifest entry that scales with the repo, or folding the audit's capability coverage into the drift number, or saying in the router and in self-verify's output that drift 0 is a floor and not a finish. All three change what an existing adopter's number means; the options are in the case.

observations.evidence: Three self-verify runs against the same untouched clone, minutes apart, with nothing about the method adopted in any of them. Manifest and pin only: `drift 17 - 37% adopted (10/27)`. Plus the eight guard scripts: `drift 14 - 68% adopted (30/44)`. Plus the rest of the copy class (SPEC.md, .claude/skills, .claude/hooks, scripts/spec, scripts/lib, .gitleaks.toml, .nvmrc, docs/facts.example.json): `drift 10 - 82% adopted (47/57)`. The percentage more than doubled and the denominator grew by 30, purely from copying files the standard itself ships - every one of which passes its own content hash by construction. Six more entries passed on files matomo already had for its own reasons: `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `SECURITY.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `AGENTS.md` - written for a different agent system entirely - and `CLAUDE.md`, which resolves through its `AGENTS.md` altPath. The comparison that makes it concrete: FIELD-1's 78-file boilerplate read `drift 14 - 56% (18/32)` at its equivalent point, so the nineteen-year platform with no specs, no records and no personas scored 82% against the boilerplate's 56%.
observations.waiver: Open, with the options written out rather than guessed. Either the adoption percentage excludes copy-class entries from its numerator until the fill-from-repo entries are authored, or it reports two numbers (what the standard supplied, what this repo authored), or the verdict line says which of the two it is measuring. All three change the number for every existing adopter, so the choice is the owner's.

observations.evidence: The shipped `.github/workflows/spec-guard.yml` runs four guard steps. The router's step 3 offers three options for landing it - accept red CI, hold until the final wave, or set the self-verify step to `--warn` - and all three concern the first step only. The last step is `node scripts/spec-guard.mjs --audit --block`, whose own comment says it is 'deliberately blocking at every profile'. On this repo that step exits 1 today and will keep exiting 1 until backlog item SPEC-12 closes, because it reports one problem per mapped capability without a spec, and there are twelve. Landing the workflow as shipped therefore fails every unrelated pull request in a repository that took 861 commits from 38 authors in the last twelve months - which is precisely the outcome the router's own paragraph exists to prevent ('That is how an adoption gets reverted and never retried'). The adoption landed the workflow with that step advisory and recorded the deviation in the file and in the backlog, but that adaptation is the adopter's invention, not one of the offered options.
observations.waiver: Open. The fix is a fourth option in the router's step 3 covering the audit step - land it advisory and flip it to --block at the last spec - plus a place to record which posture was chosen. Cheap, but it is a change to what the shipped workflow means on merge, so it is proposed rather than made.

observations.evidence: `.nvmrc` is a `copy` entry carrying a `sha256`, so its content is the standard's and any change is drift unless recorded as a `content` exception. Its content is `24.18.0`. matomo's `package.json` declares `engines.node` `>=16.0.0 <17.0.0`, and six committed CI steps pin `node-version: '16'` or `'12'` (`buildvue.yml:85`, `matomo-tests.yml:319/335/403/438`, `run-single-ui-test-suite.yml:50`). A repo has one `.nvmrc`; it cannot say both what runs the guards and what runs the application. Copying it verbatim tells every contributor to use a runtime `npm install` rejects. The entry is `required: false`, so this adoption resolved it by not carrying the file at all - self-verify then reports `.nvmrc absent (optional)` and adds no drift, which is the honest outcome but leaves nothing declaring the Node the guards need. The general shape: an entry whose content is by definition the adopting repo's own is classed `copy`.
observations.waiver: Open. Reclassing .nvmrc from copy to merge or fill-from-repo is a one-line manifest change, but it removes a content hash from an entry that has one, which is a deliberate weakening of the check for every repo that has no Node of its own. The alternative - declaring the guards' runtime somewhere other than .nvmrc - is a larger design change. Both are in the case.

observations.evidence: matomo owns a database. `core/Db/Schema/Mysql.php:51` `getTablesCreateSql()` returns 30 `CREATE TABLE` statements - `user`, `access`, `user_token_auth`, `log_visit`, `log_link_visit_action`, `log_conversion`, `archive_numeric`, `archive_blob` and the rest - and 179 forward-only update scripts under `core/Updates/` change them over time. There is no `database/schema/` directory and no typed twin. `node scripts/schema-pair.mjs --block` prints `schema-pair: no database/schema/ - skipping (R24 binds repos that own a database)` and exits 0. The skip condition is the absence of the directory the rule requires you to create, which is the state of every repo that has not complied with R24 - so the guard can only ever fail a pair that has already been built, never the failure to build one. Confirmed that nothing else covers it: the manifest has no `files` entry whose path contains `database`, and the only entries citing rule R24 are `scripts/schema-pair.mjs` and the guard itself. The repo therefore reaches drift 0 with R24 wholly unmet and a green guard line. Matomo's shape is also a genuine argument against R24 as written - the DDL interpolates a runtime table prefix and three engine subclasses share one source - which is recorded as ADR-005 in the adopted repo and as backlog item GUARD-6, so this is a rule that needs both a check and a shape discussion, not just a check.
observations.waiver: Open, and deliberately not patched here: making schema-pair fail on a missing database/schema/ requires a way to tell a repo that owns a database from one that does not, and getting that wrong turns every library into a failing repo. The options are a manifest files entry gated on a declared 'owns a database' flag, a detector (CREATE TABLE in tracked source), or a recorded R7 answer that the repo owns no database. matomo's own shape (runtime table prefix, three engine subclasses) is also an argument about R24 itself, not only about its guard.

observations.evidence: Measured twice. First, a naive `$unclaimed` (docs, scripts, .github, .claude) against an early map: `spec-guard --audit: 13516 problem(s)`, of which 13,515 were unclaimed files and 1 was a capability without a spec - one count for two different kinds of defect. The list printed the first 20 in git order and `... and 13495 more`; because git order is alphabetical, all 20 shown were `.ddev/*` - the least consequential paths in the repository. Second, after the real 14-capability map and a considered `$unclaimed` (tests, libs, node_modules, misc, config, .ddev, .github, .claude, docs, scripts, plugins/Example*, root files): 296 unclaimed files, still printed as 20 paths plus a remainder. Rolling the same 296 up by directory - the guard already has the list - changes the picture completely: **150 of them are `plugins/CoreHome`**, the one directory that straddles three capabilities, and the rest are small `core/` subtrees. The information needed to act was in the guard's own data and not in its output. Speed is not the problem and should be said plainly: that run took 82 ms.
observations.waiver: Open, and the cheapest of the round: the guard already has the data, so a per-directory rollup plus separating the unclaimed count from the map-defect count is presentation only, with no verdict or exit-code change. Not made this round because it touches a shipped guard's output and its test, and this round's budget went to the adoption itself.

observations.evidence: matomo's own `.gitattributes` happens to set `text eol=lf`, so `git check-attr text eol -- .claude/hooks/lib.sh` reported `text: set` / `eol: lf` and the guards were safe by luck rather than by check. Replacing it with `* text=auto` + `*.sh text eol=crlf` + `*.mjs text eol=crlf` - confirmed with `git check-attr eol`, which then reported `crlf` for both `scripts/self-verify.mjs` and `.claude/hooks/lib.sh` - left self-verify printing `PASS file .gitattributes (forces LF on the shipped bash guards and Node scripts - a repo whose own setting is eol=crlf makes every hook exit 127 with empty stdout, which for a deny-guard is silence, not a refusal)`. The PASS line describes, word for word, the state the repo was in. The entry is `merge` class with no `requiredKeys`, and it could not have any: self-verify's key check handles JSON and YAML only and fails an entry that declares keys on any other format. So the entry SHAPE-08 added to stop silent hook failure asserts only that a file with that name exists.
observations.waiver: Open. self-verify would have to ask git (`git check-attr eol -- <paths>`), which introduces a git dependency into a check that currently has none and needs a defined behaviour when there is no git - a degit'd tree is a supported state. Warning rather than failing is the safer half of the fix; both are in the case.

observations.evidence: The adopted workflow was adapted rather than copied (a declared `permissions:` block, an explicit node version, the audit step left advisory), and the deviation was recorded as `{ "kind": "content", "match": ".github/workflows/spec-guard.yml", "reason": "..." }`. self-verify answered `WARN exception content:.github/workflows/spec-guard.yml is excepted but met anyway - delete the exception, it is describing a deviation this repo no longer has`. The repo does have the deviation. The mechanism cannot see it: `verifyContent` returns immediately when an entry has no `sha256`, and a `merge` entry never has one, so the exception is never consumed and falls into the stale-exception branch. The message then instructs the adopter to delete a true record. The exception was removed and the deviation now lives only in a comment in the workflow and in the adopted backlog - which is the outcome R17 exists to prevent.
observations.waiver: Open, message-only. self-verify already knows each entry's adapt class, so the stale-exception branch could say 'a merge entry carries no recorded content, so a content exception on it can never apply' instead of asserting the deviation is gone. Minor enough that it should ride with whichever change touches the exception machinery next.

observations.evidence: matomo already carries a 124-line `AGENTS.md`, written for AI coding agents, whose `## Matomo Agent Skills` section routes fifteen kinds of work to skills held in a **different repository** (`matomo-org/matomo-agent-skills`), and which says outright that `AGENTS.md` 'cannot install or enable external skills by itself'. Two consequences the procedure has no step for. First, the manifest classes `AGENTS.md` as `fill-from-repo`, so the file's presence passed from the first run - the standard's very first required entry was satisfied by a file written for another system, and only the three required headings caught anything. Second, this is R3's failure mode in its most defensible form: the operational rules are versioned, reviewed and public, just not in this repository - and R22 requires the lifecycle procedures to ship in the repo in a form its agent can execute. The router's step 3 says 'Put conventions in AGENTS.md (single source)', which assumes there is nothing there. The adoption merged - matomo's content kept verbatim, the altitude ladder and the two required behaviour sections added around it - but that is an adopter's judgement call on the standard's own first rule.
observations.waiver: Open. The intake needs a step for an existing agent entry point - read it, keep it, and name the out-of-repo rules as an R3 finding rather than overwriting or ignoring them. Writing that step is a prose change to the router; deciding whether a substantive pre-existing AGENTS.md should still satisfy a fill-from-repo entry on presence alone is not, and that is the half left open.

observations.evidence: Six records were written into the shipped `adr/` + `bdr/` split and both indexes were filled at the same time - the failure DOC-18 covers was avoided. `decision-records-check --block` still reported all six as `has no row in ... README.md`, because the index rows had been written as `| ADR-001 | [title](file.md) | Accepted |`. The guard accepts `[NNN](file.md)` or a bare `NNN` in the first cell and nothing else; the guard's own source comment names that convention, and the shipped `adr/README.md` an adopter is filling does not - its only row is the placeholder `| - | (none yet) | - |` under the header `| # | Title | Status |`, so the natural first cell for an ADR index is the one that fails. Rewriting the six rows to `| [001](file.md) | title | Accepted |` produced `decision-records-check: OK (6 record(s), index and directory agree)`. Minor, and the guard did its job - but it is a first-adoption stumble on a file whose whole purpose is to be filled in by someone reading it for the first time.
observations.waiver: Open. Naming the row format in the shipped adr/README.md and bdr/README.md prose is a two-line docs change. It was left rather than made because the obvious form - a commented-out example row, the way the backlog template does it - would be read as a real row by decision-records-check (it scans every line beginning with a pipe, comments included), so the fix has to be prose or it has to touch the parser.

observations.evidence: Re-run at a size FIELD-1's first target could not test. The engine did not crash, guess or fall back to the skeleton on a 13,591-file repository it had never seen: it went `drift 17 - 37% adopted (10/27)` on the untouched clone through `drift 14`, `drift 10`, `drift 3`, `drift 2` to `self-verify: OK - drift 0 - 98% adopted (57/58), 1 excepted`, and every intermediate number was reproducible. One entry was closed by a recorded exception rather than by an artifact, which is R17 working: matomo writes each change under the heading of the release it will ship in (`## Matomo 5.13.0`, while `core/Version.php:25` reads `5.13.0-alpha`), so that heading is its unreleased section under a name nineteen years of contributors already use - adding an `## Unreleased` heading nobody writes under would have satisfied the check with an empty section. The exception cost coverage exactly as designed: 98%, never 100%. What this pass does not carry is any claim that drift 0 means the repository is aligned - see ADOPT-12.

The onboarding phase's shortcut - 'a library, CLI or framework's existing package/crate boundary is often already the capability map' - is at its most tempting here and would have been wrong: 98 plugin directories are 98 units of deployment, and the qualifier that stops it ('confirm the boundary is behavior-shaped') held. Reading behaviour instead produced 14 capabilities, and the three largest directories each straddle more than one: `plugins/CoreHome` (457 files) carries the Vue component library (reporting-ui), the core visit-identity dimensions `Columns/VisitorId.php`, `VisitIp.php`, `VisitorFingerprint.php` and `Tracker/VisitRequestProcessor.php` (visit-enrichment), and `LoginAllowlist.php` (access-control); `plugins/Actions` and `plugins/Referrers` each hold a tracking-time processor and a reporting-time archiver. The map splits CoreHome by subdirectory for that reason. `spec-guard --audit` confirmed every one of the 14 capabilities' globs matches at least one file - no empty globs - including the 16 top-level plugin directories that are git submodules (17 gitlinks under `plugins/` counting `plugins/Morpheus/icons`), which appear as single entries and therefore take a bare path with no `/**`.

The churn pass was run on real history rather than skipped or faked: the clone was `git clone --filter=blob:none`, which omits historical blobs but keeps every commit and tree, so `git log --since=2025-08-06 --name-only` ranks hotspots normally. It returned `plugins/TagManager` (61 touches), `plugins/CoreHome/vue/dist/CoreHome.umd.js` (49), `plugins/CustomAlerts` (36), `core/Version.php` (29), `plugins/PrivacyManager/PrivacyManager.php` (25). Two things worth stating rather than glossing: two of those five (`plugins/TagManager`, `plugins/CustomAlerts`) are gitlinks, so their churn is a submodule pointer bump and not code in this repository; and the 49 touches on a committed build artefact are a signal about the release shape, not about behaviour. The pass's shallow-clone caveat is the right one and a blobless clone is not caught by it - worth noting for the next run that 'has real history' and 'has real file contents' are different properties, and only the first is needed here.

Five retroactive ADRs and one BDR were authored into the shipped `adr/` + `bdr/` split, each stating what the code chose with the file and line proving it - the PHP 7.2 floor (`composer.json` `config.platform.php` `7.2.9` plus `core/testMinimumPhpVersion.php:24`, against 16 waived Twig advisories), browser-triggered archiving on by default (`config/global.ini.php:398`), the cron archiver calling its own HTTP API (`core/CronArchive.php:802`), the reflection-published Web API (`core/Plugin/API.php:22-23`, `core/API/Proxy.php:700`), and the PHP-literal schema with forward-only updates (`core/Db/Schema/Mysql.php:51`). The BDR was left `Proposed` rather than `Accepted` on purpose: it is the one record the code cannot settle - who wins a tie between the tracked end user and the operator - and two shipped defaults contradict the reading the mission statement implies. `decision-records-check --block` ended at `OK (6 record(s), index and directory agree)` after the row-format correction recorded in DOC-19.

Guard cost measured on the adopted 13,591-file tree, best of three runs each, wall clock: self-verify 218 ms, spec-structure 64 ms, facts-check 40 ms, schema-pair 40 ms, sprint-guard 42 ms, decision-records-check 43 ms, `spec-guard --audit` 76 ms, `spec-guard` (diff mode) 113 ms. Nothing is close to the minute that would make a guard one nobody runs, and self-verify - the only one above 150 ms, and the only one that spawns the other guards as subprocesses - measured 240 ms on the unadopted clone before any of them had work to do, so its cost is not growing with what the repository carries. Two consecutive self-verify runs on the adopted tree produced byte-identical 84-line output (`diff` reported no difference). The scale worry this case exists to catch does not apply to these guards, which is worth publishing as loudly as the failures: every defect in this round is about what the output says, never about what it cost to produce.
